    The punctum

    In 1980, in a small book called Camera Lucida, the French thinker Roland Barthes tried to name why some photographs stop us cold while thousands of others slide past unnoticed. He landed on two words.

    Studium, the part you can explain

    The studium is everything in a photograph you can read, discuss, and understand through what you already know. The subject, the setting, the historical moment, the photographer's obvious intention. It is the interest you take in an image because you recognise what it is about. Barthes called this a kind of polite, educated interest, real but cool. You can teach the studium. You can write an essay about it. Most photographs offer only this, and Barthes called them unary: they shout or inform, but they do not wound.

    Punctum, the part that pierces you

    The punctum is different. The word is Latin for a wound, a prick, a mark left by a pointed instrument. It is the detail that leaps out of the picture and pierces you personally, not because it is important or well composed, but because for reasons you often cannot explain, it catches. As Barthes wrote, it is this element which rises from the scene, shoots out of it like an arrow, and pierces me.

    The punctum is usually small and almost always accidental, something the photographer never intended you to fixate on. A pair of hands. A child's shoes. A crack of light. And it is personal: what wounds you may leave the person beside you completely untouched. What I can name cannot really prick me, Barthes noted. The moment you fully explain it, it stops being a punctum and becomes studium again.

    Why this game

    When you play Punctum, you are not judging whether a photo is good, or well made, or important. You are noticing something quieter and harder to fake: whether it reaches out and touches you. There is no wrong answer, and yours does not have to match anyone else's. The point is to slow down enough to feel the difference between a photograph you understand and one that gets under your skin. That distinction is the beginning of learning to look like an artist rather than a viewer.

    Barthes found his own most piercing photograph was one of his mother as a child, an image so private he refused to print it in the book. The punctum, in the end, is where a photograph stops being about everyone and becomes about you.

    The cull

    Anyone can take a photograph. The photographer's real work often begins afterwards, in the ruthless, clarifying act of deciding which few images survive. Learning to cull is learning to see your own work the way an artist does.

    The edit is where the artist appears

    A body of work, a portfolio, an exhibition, a photobook, is almost never a single image. It is a group, and a group is only as strong as its weakest picture. One mediocre frame left in to fill space quietly drags down everything around it. Professional editors have a blunt rule for the hesitation you will feel: if you are not sure whether an image belongs, that doubt is your answer. It goes.

    Kill your darlings

    The hardest cuts are the photos you love for reasons the viewer will never see, because of how hard it was to get, or the memory attached to it, or the effort it cost. None of that is visible in the frame. The fine art photographer learns to separate the story behind the picture from what the picture actually delivers to a stranger's eye. Culling means being honest about that gap, again and again.

    Choose against your best, not against the rest

    When you cull, do not ask whether a photo is decent. Almost all of them are decent. Ask whether it is stronger than the one beside it. That is exactly what this game forces: two images, one choice, no way to keep both. Each duel is a small, honest confrontation. Do it enough times and only the images with real force are left standing. Then you rank them, because even among your strongest there is an order, a single image that carries the most.

    What you are training

    Editing this way builds the muscle every serious photographer relies on: the ability to look at your own work coldly, to prefer five true images over twenty comfortable ones, and to trust your eye under pressure. The photographs you keep say something. So do the ones you are brave enough to let go.

    Edit ruthlessly. It is the most common advice in fine art photography, and the hardest to follow, because it asks you to be a clear eyed critic of the thing you are most attached to. That is the skill this game is quietly teaching.
